name: Iowa
summary_text: A trans visitor to Iowa stands under the United States federal framework on travel documents and screening. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, and prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. The Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect in November 2025, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad; the ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records. Screening at US checkpoints carries an outing risk. TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that are invasive of privacy, and multiple foreign governments have responded: in April 2025 several countries issued advisories about trans people travelling to the United States over identity-document and data rules, and in March 2025 at least eight European governments, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the country. Visa decisions follow the same federal framing: since February 2025 the State Department has flagged visa applicants with an internal marking and treats applicants who list a gender other than their assigned sex as grounds for a permanent ban on grounds of fraud, alongside a ban on trans athletes entering to compete in women's sports. In Iowa itself, the sharpest facility rule applies to schools. Senate File 482, signed by Governor Kim Reynolds on 22 March 2023, requires anyone on Iowa school grounds, including students, staff, parents and visitors, to use only restrooms and changing areas corresponding with the biological sex listed on a birth certificate. The restriction covers multiperson restrooms and locker rooms at public and private elementary and secondary schools and took effect immediately. A visitor entering an Iowa school building is therefore bound by it. Single-person facilities remain available to trans students who obtain written consent from legal guardians. Iowa also bars gender-affirming care for minors. Senate File 538, signed the same day, prevents doctors from administering puberty blockers, hormone therapy and transition-related surgery to anyone under 18, which constrains care access for a trans visitor under 18 travelling with family. At federal level, Executive Order 14187 (January 2025) described gender-affirming care for minors as "chemical and surgical mutilation of children," the Department of Justice subpoenaed records of patients under 19 from over 20 hospitals in summer 2025, specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline were shut down in July 2025, and October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. Gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states. Several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court. The Movement Advancement Project equality map catalogues state bans on transgender people's use of public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity, and lists Iowa's enacted facility ban. Iowa sits in an 18-state group defining sex as biological sex, but is not listed among the states that define sex by birth in statute. Under Erin In The Morning's Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map of July 2026, Iowa is graded in "The Worst States" group, one tier below the four "Do Not Travel" states. Federal custody also presents documented harm: from 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted policies mandating conversion therapy for transgender inmates, the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025, and in December 2025 the Attorney General instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists characterised as "domestic terrorist groups."

name: Kansas
summary_text: Kansas visitors stand under two layers: the United States federal framework, which applies in every state, and Kansas Senate Bill 244, enacted in late February 2026. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, defined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, and required federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department stopped processing the X marker, issues new passports only as M or F from the supporting documents submitted, and leaves passports already issued with an X valid until they expire. The Supreme Court allowed those passport restrictions to take effect in November 2025. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records.  Entry and screening carry their own exposure. Visa applicants who list a gender other than sex assigned at birth can be treated as grounds for a permanent fraud-based ban, and applicants flagged as trans athletes are marked internally, under a State Department rule announced in February 2025. TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that are invasive of privacy, which creates a risk of being outed at the checkpoint.  Within Kansas, the sharpest document risk is the state licence. Senate Bill 244 bars changing the gender marker on a Kansas driver's licence or state ID and invalidates existing licences whose marker is inconsistent with sex assigned at birth. The Kansas Department of Revenue has been mailing written notice, and many holders have already been told their licence is now invalid. A trans visitor holding or renewing a Kansas licence should expect it to be treated as void for identification and driving purposes; a federal passport remains the more reliable document, subject to the federal marker rules above.  The same law confines trans people to facilities designated for sex assigned at birth and creates new civil and criminal penalties. It also lets private individuals sue trans people encountered in facilities designated for the other sex, a private right of action that civil-rights groups describe as a bounty mechanism. On 20 February 2026 a national legal-risk assessment moved Kansas from its Worst Laws tier to Do Not Travel, the first state placed on that tier in a year, citing the new bathroom-bounty law and the interstate-travel exposure that follows from it.  Litigation is under way. Doe v. State of Kansas was filed in Douglas County District Court within days of the law's enactment by two transgender men represented by the ACLU of Kansas and Ballard Spahr, who cite fear of violence under the bathroom-restriction and ID-invalidation provisions. The case was pending as reported, and no ruling on the law's validity had issued.  Care access is constrained for a visitor who needs it. Executive Order 14187 of January 2025 described gender-affirming care for minors as chemical and surgical mutilation of children, prompting some hospitals to pause care, and in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed more than 20 hospitals for full records of patients under 19. In July 2025 the federal government shut down specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, and October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. Several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court.

sources.title: SB 244 (Kansas, 2026)
sources.documents: Requires state IDs including driver's licenses to reflect sex assigned at birth; requires invalidation and reissue at holder's expense; mandates up to $1,000 financial and criminal penalties for using gender-segregated facility in publicly-owned building not matching sex assigned at birth plus $1,000 bounty-hunter private right to sue
sources.detail: Passed via veto override over Gov. Laura Kelly, took effect immediately Feb 26, 2026; holders received surrender letters warning of penalties for operating without valid credential; ACLU of Kansas filed lawsuit to block

sources.title: Kansas Court of Appeals ruling - June 13, 2025
sources.documents: Unanimous reversal of injunction prohibiting gender identity changes to driver's licenses; holds Kobach failed to show irreparable harm from KDOR long-standing policy
sources.detail: Reversed Judge Teresa Watson temporary restraining order citing public safety concern; found error of fact that law enforcement would be hindered if license did not display sex assigned at birth; remanded to Shawnee District Court for reassessment
